c.tagline: White-walled old town by day, world capital of clubbing by night.

taxi.fareNote: Metered within town, but fixed/regulated flat fares apply for set routes like the airport; official fare sheets are posted in every cab. Demand far outstrips supply in peak summer season and at night, especially around club closing times. Uber operates on the island but only via licensed VTC drivers booked through the app — there's no street-hail Uber.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that connects to police, fire, and ambulance across Spain; the Guardia Civil and Policia Local also operate island-wide.

hood_landmark.Sant Antoni de Portmany: Sant Antoni de Portmany sunset strip Ibiza
hood_landmark.Santa Eulària des Riu: Santa Eularia des Riu marina Ibiza

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing and drink-spiking in the club/nightlife zones (San Antonio)

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled hilltop old town (Dalt Vila) and the harborside Marina/Sa Penya district below it, packed with cathedral views, boutique galleries, tapas bars and late-night terraces; best for first-timers who want history, dining and nightlife within walking distance.

Ibiza's biggest party strip, a long sandy beach lined with superclubs like Ushuàia and Hì Ibiza and beach clubs blasting music from midday on; suits clubbers and groups who want to be inside the action, less so anyone seeking quiet.

The island's sunset-worship capital on the west coast, famous for Café del Mar and a strip of bars along Carrer d'Es Egipte plus a separate quieter bay (S'Arenal/Es Pujols); popular with younger, budget-conscious nightlife travelers.

A cosmopolitan, more laid-back resort town on the east coast with a marina, family-friendly beaches, a Sunday hippy-market heritage and strong local Spanish character; suits couples, families and travelers wanting good restaurants without full-on clubbing.

A relaxed east-coast beach village built around a broad sandy bay, known for its Wednesday hippy market and calmer pace than the south or west coasts; suits families and travelers who want beach time over nightlife.

water.note: Tap water meets EU standards and is safe to drink, though it can taste salty or mineral-heavy.

transit.pay: Pay in cash directly to the driver (typically €1.50-€3.60 depending on distance); there is no rechargeable island-wide transit card. Some routes also allow online ticket purchase in advance during peak season.
transit.hours: Daytime routes run roughly 6:30am-10pm; a limited seasonal night bus network (Disco Bus) links Ibiza Town, Playa d'en Bossa, Sant Antoni and the main clubs from around midnight to 6am, June-September only.
transit.note: Buses connect Ibiza Town with Sant Antoni, Santa Eulària, the airport and beach towns, but service thins out sharply outside peak season and away from the main routes; a rental car, taxi or scooter is the practical way to reach quieter coves and villages.

train: Ibiza is an island with no railway; there are no trains.
bus: No international or mainland coach routes exist from an island

transit.m: Bus lines 10/10E to Ibiza Town, 20-30 min

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% at restaurants for good service is common and appreciated, more so in tourist-oriented restaurants and clubs.

food.name: Bullit de peix
food.desc: Ibiza's great fishermen's dish: rock fish poached with potato and allioli, then the broth used to cook a second course of arros a banda.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: Vara de Rey institution open since 1934, the reference point for island cooking.

places.name: Es Torrent
places.note: Beachfront seafood restaurant famous for fish bought off the day's boats.

places.name: S'Illa des Bosc
places.note: Sunset terrace over Cala Conta with a well-known bullit and rice courses.

food.name: Sofrit pages
food.desc: Peasant one-pot of chicken, lamb, sobrassada and butifarra slow-cooked with potato, saffron and island spices. Traditionally a feast-day dish.

places.name: Can Caus
places.note: Farm restaurant using its own meat and cheese; the most reliable sofrit on the island.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: Cooks the old recipes properly; book ahead as the dining room fills fast.

places.name: Es Ventall
places.note: Long-running kitchen that rethinks Ibizan classics with local produce.

food.name: Arros de matances
food.desc: Rich baked rice from the old pig-slaughter feasts, made with pork, sobrassada, chicken and almonds. Filling, and usually cooked for two.

places.name: Can Caus
places.note: Country dining room where island families go for big shared rice dishes.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: Rotates traditional rices through the week; ask what is on that day.

places.name: Es Ventall
places.note: Seasonal menu with a strong line in Ibizan rices and countryside dishes.

food.name: Frita de polp
food.desc: Octopus fried down with potato, peppers, garlic and a hit of paprika until the edges caramelise. Served as a sharing plate.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: One of the dishes regulars order every visit; generous and properly seasoned.

places.name: Es Torrent
places.note: Seafood specialist with octopus straight off the local boats.

places.name: S'Illa des Bosc
places.note: Good sharing plates before the rice courses, with a view over the islets.

food.name: Ensalada payesa amb peix sec
food.desc: Country salad of potato, tomato, onion and green pepper topped with flakes of sun-dried ray or skate, dressed in olive oil.

places.name: Bar Costa
places.note: Village bar hung with hams and paintings, a fixture since the 1950s.

places.name: Can Caus
places.note: Uses its own farm vegetables; a good introduction to rural Ibizan food.

places.name: Es Ventall
places.note: Modern take on the salad using dried fish cured on the island.

food.name: Flao
food.desc: Ibiza's signature dessert: a thin pastry case filled with fresh goat cheese, egg, aniseed and mint, baked and dusted with sugar.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: Homemade version with a pronounced mint note, the way islanders expect it.

places.name: Can Caus
places.note: Made with cheese from the farm's own goats, sold by the slice or whole.

places.name: Bar Costa
places.note: Casual place to finish a village lunch with flao and a herb liqueur.

food.name: Hierbas ibicencas
food.desc: Anise-based herbal liqueur macerated with thyme, rosemary, fennel and juniper picked on the island. Drunk ice-cold after dinner.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: House bottle appears on the table at the end of the meal, as tradition dictates.

places.name: Bar Costa
places.note: Village bar with several island brands, including small home-macerated batches.

places.name: Can Caus
places.note: Shop-restaurant that also sells local hierbas and sobrassada to take away.

food.name: Cafe caleta
food.desc: Ibizan flamed coffee laced with brandy, rum, cinnamon, lemon peel and sugar, served in a clay pot. Strong, sweet and theatrical.

places.name: Ca n'Alfredo
places.note: The classic old-town address for the traditional clay-pot preparation.

places.name: Es Ventall
places.note: Rounds off a long dinner with a well-made caleta for the table.

places.name: Bar Costa
places.note: Unpretentious village setting for the island's after-dinner coffee ritual.

landmarks: Dalt Vila (Ibiza Old Town)
This UNESCO-listed walled hilltop old town of cobbled lanes and Renaissance fortifications has crowned Ibiza Town for centuries and remains its most photographed skyline.
Ibiza Cathedral (Catedral de Santa Maria)
Perched at the summit of Dalt Vila, this Gothic-Baroque cathedral offers sweeping panoramic views over the old town, harbor, and the shimmering Mediterranean.
Café del Mar Sunset Strip
The birthplace of the sunset-lounge scene, this beachfront café in San Antonio draws crowds nightly to applaud as the sun dips dramatically into the sea.
Ses Salines Natural Park
Ancient salt flats turned protected wetland where flocks of pink flamingos wade beside pristine dunes and turquoise water, a favorite for nature photographers.
Portinatx
A postcard-perfect cluster of sheltered coves on the island's rugged north coast, prized for calm turquoise waters framed by dramatic rocky headlands.
Santa Eulària des Riu
A charming whitewashed town on Ibiza's east coast, known for its hilltop church, palm-lined promenade, and the island's only permanent river.
Puig des Molins Necropolis
One of the most important Phoenician-Punic burial sites in the Mediterranean, this UNESCO-recognized ancient necropolis reveals over 2,500 years of island history.
Ibiza Town Harbour
The bustling waterfront where superyachts moor beneath the illuminated ramparts of Dalt Vila, offering one of the island's classic postcard views at dusk.
Platja d'en Bossa
Ibiza's longest beach, a 2.7-kilometre sweep of sand just south of the harbour lined with hotels, beach clubs and the open-air superclub Ushuaïa.
Passeig de Vara de Rey
Ibiza Town's grand pedestrian promenade, lined with early-20th-century Art Nouveau buildings and centred on the 1904 statue of General Vara de Rey.

train.note: Ibiza is an island, so there is no rail service at all - no international, mainland, or local trains.

bus.note: No international or mainland coach routes exist from an island. The aIBIZAbus network (run by the Consell d'Eivissa) covers the island itself, linking Ibiza Town with Sant Antoni, Santa Eulària, the airport and beach towns.

ferry.note: There are no international ferries from Ibiza. Balearia, Trasmed and GNV (https://www.balearia.com/en) sail from the Port of Ibiza (Ibiza Town) to the Spanish mainland (Barcelona ~8-9h overnight or faster by fast ferry; Valencia and Denia ~3.5-6h) and to Palma de Mallorca (~2-4h) - all domestic Spanish routes. The short, frequent hop to Formentera (~25-40 min, run by Trasmapi, Balearia, Formentera Lines and Mediterrania-Pitiusa from both the Port of Ibiza and the Port of Sant Antoni, https://www.trasmapi.com/en) is the most popular day trip and runs year-round; mainland routes reduce frequency outside summer.

half.name: Es Vedrà & Cala d'Hort
half.blurb: A dramatic uninhabited limestone islet rising from the sea, best viewed at sunset from the beach at Cala d'Hort.

half.name: Cala Comte & Cala Bassa
half.blurb: Turquoise coves on the west coast famous for calm swimming water and postcard sunsets, easily reached by bus or boat from Sant Antoni.

half.name: Cuevas de Can Marcà & Port de Sant Miquel
half.blurb: A cave system on the north coast with stalactites and an underground pool, paired with a quiet cove and cliffside village.

half.name: Hippy Market at Es Canà or Las Dalias
half.blurb: Ibiza's counterculture heritage lives on at these open-air markets of handmade jewelry, clothing and local crafts.

full.name: Formentera
full.blurb: A short ferry ride from Ibiza Town or Sant Antoni delivers pine-scented dunes and the turquoise, Caribbean-like waters of Ses Illetes beach.
